title: Philippians
subtitle: Joy in chains, and the mind of Christ
lead: Philippians is a letter from Paul, written in prison, to the church he had founded some years earlier in Philippi, a Roman colony in northern Greece. The Philippians had sent him money and a helper, Epaphroditus. Paul writes back to thank them, to tell them how he is, and to urge them to stand together. Although he may be facing death, the letter is full of joy: the words 'joy' and 'rejoice' come about sixteen times in four short chapters.

At its center is the passage often called the Christ hymn (2:6-11): Christ, being in the form of God, emptied himself, took a slave's form, died on a cross, and was raised by God to the name above every name. Paul offers this as the pattern for the church's life together. The letter also holds Paul's own story of giving up his status for Christ (3:4-14), the hope of citizens of heaven (3:20-21), and some of the most loved lines in the Bible ('For me, living is Christ and dying is gain'; 'Rejoice in the Lord at all times'; 'I have strength for everything in the one who makes me strong').
facts: Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender (1:1). Almost all scholars accept Paul as the author.
If written from Rome, about AD 62; from Ephesus, about AD 52-55; from Caesarea, about AD 57-59. See 'Where was Paul in prison?' on the chapter 1 page.
A prison (1:7, 13-14). Rome is the traditional view; Ephesus and Caesarea are also proposed.
The church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia: mostly Gentile believers, with overseers and deacons (1:1), women co-workers (4:2-3), and a long partnership with Paul (4:15-16).
A letter of friendship and thanks, with a warning section (chapter 3) and a poetic passage about Christ (2:6-11). Some scholars hold that it joins two or three shorter letters.
authorship: It opens 'From Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus' (1:1) and speaks in Paul's voice throughout, with his personal story (3:4-6), his imprisonment and his co-workers.

Philippians is one of the letters almost all scholars agree Paul wrote, together with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Its style, its personal details and its early use support this. Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to the same church in the second century, recalls that Paul 'when he was absent wrote letters to you' (Philippians 3.2 in Kirsopp Lake's translation; Roberts and Donaldson translate 'a letter'), and that the Philippians were praised 'in the beginning of his Epistle' (11).

Many scholars since the nineteenth century have held that our Philippians joins two or three letters. One common proposal: Letter A, a thank-you note (4:10-20); Letter B, 1:1-3:1 with perhaps 4:4-9 and 4:21-23; Letter C, a warning letter, 3:2-4:1 with perhaps 4:2-3 (Philip Sellew among others). Their evidence: the sudden change of tone at 3:2 after 'As for the rest' (3:1); thanks for the gift coming only at the end; and Polycarp's plural 'letters'. Others defend one letter: 'As for the rest' often means 'so then' in Paul; the same words and themes run through all four chapters (think, form, low, citizenship, joy, partnership); and the gift is mentioned at the start (1:5). The Plain translates the letter as it stands.

Since Ernst Lohmeyer (1928) many scholars have held that 2:6-11 is an earlier Christian hymn or creed that Paul quotes, perhaps adding 'yes, death on a cross'. Others think Paul composed it. The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls it 'a hymn cited by St. Paul' (461).

audience.to: The church at Philippi, the first church Paul founded in Europe, about AD 49 or 50 (Acts 16). Philippi was a Roman colony, refounded after the battle of 42 BC and settled with Roman veterans, whose people were proud to be Roman (Acts 16:21). The church began with Lydia, a Gentile dealer in purple cloth who worshiped Israel's God, and the women at a place of prayer by a river, then the jailer and his household (Acts 16:13-34). By the time of the letter it had overseers and deacons (1:1), women co-workers of Paul such as Euodia and Syntyche (4:2-3), and other co-workers like Clement (4:3). It was mostly Gentile and probably mostly poor (2 Corinthians 8:2 speaks of the Macedonian churches' 'deep poverty'), though some, like Lydia, had means. It had supported Paul from the start, more than any other church (4:15-16), and had just sent Epaphroditus with a gift (2:25; 4:18). The church faced opposition in the city (1:28-30), a quarrel between leaders (4:2), and opponents Paul warns against in chapter 3 (3:2), most often read as teachers who would require circumcision.
audience.why: Paul writes for several reasons at once: to thank them for the gift without becoming their client (4:10-20); to tell them how he is and why his chains have helped the good news (1:12-26); to send back Epaphroditus, who had nearly died, and to praise him (2:25-30); to announce visits by Timothy and himself (2:19-24); to warn them about the opponents of chapter 3 (3:2-21); and above all to call them to unity and humility, the 'mind of Christ' (1:27-2:11; 4:2-3). Knowing the readers changes the reading. In a Roman colony that prized status, citizenship and the emperor as 'lord' and 'savior', Paul's language of living as citizens (1:27), of a commonwealth in heaven (3:20), of a slave's form (2:7) and of every knee bowing to Jesus as Lord (2:10-11) had a sharp local edge. If, as most readers think, those opponents wanted Gentile believers circumcised, chapter 3 answers the question of who belongs to God's people (see the views). And a church whose leaders were quarreling explains why the center of the letter is a hymn about the one who did not use his status for himself.
views: Paul writes during the custody of Acts 28, about AD 62. The 'praetorium' is the Praetorian Guard and 'Caesar's household' the imperial staff in the capital. A church with overseers and deacons (1:1) and a prisoner expecting a verdict that could mean death (1:20-23) suit this later date. The traditional view, given in the Textus Receptus' subscription, and often judged the most likely.

Paul writes from an imprisonment in Ephesus, about AD 52-55, not told in Acts but suggested by 2 Corinthians 11:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:32. Ephesus is much nearer Philippi, which suits the several journeys the letter implies; imperial slaves served in the provinces (Michael Flexsenhar, 2019, argues for Asia Minor).
Paul writes from Herod's Praetorium in Caesarea, about AD 57-59 (Acts 23:35; 24:27).

Most readers take 'the dogs ... the mutilation' (3:2) to be Jewish-Christian teachers who required circumcision of Gentile believers, like the agitators in Galatia; others think of local Jews, pagan cults, or Christian libertines (3:18-19). Paul says 'look out', so they may not yet have reached Philippi.

outline: Greeting to the saints, overseers and deacons
Thanks for their partnership, and a prayer
Paul's chains, the rival preachers, living and dying
Live as citizens worthy of the good news
One mind: humility and care for others
The Christ hymn: emptied, obedient, exalted
Work out your salvation; lights in the world
The warning, Paul's record, and everything as loss
Running for the prize; citizens of heaven

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Philippians against Roman Philippi: a colony of veterans proud of its citizenship, the honor culture of offices and titles, slavery, the emperor as 'lord', and the church Acts 16 describes. Asks where Paul was in prison, and what the praetorium and Caesar's household were. Joseph Hellerman's study of honor in Roman Philippi is one example.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made: whether it joins two or three letters, whether 2:6-11 is an earlier hymn (Lohmeyer and many since) or Paul's own, who the opponents of chapter 3 were, and what the Greek of the hard places (morphe, harpagmos, ekenosen, pistis Christou) means.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's shape and words: the friendship-letter form, the thread of joy, the verb 'think' (phroneo) in every chapter, the 'form' words that tie chapter 3 to the hymn, the athletic and business pictures, and the two movements of the hymn, down and up.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Philippians as a letter from a Jew who still names his tribe and his Pharisee training: the echoes of Job, Isaiah, Deuteronomy and Israel's worship; Isaiah 45:23 applied to Jesus; the meaning of 'the dogs' and 'the circumcision' (3:2-3), and the misuse of 3:2 against Jews; and the New Perspective and 'Paul within Judaism' readings of 3:5-9.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads how the churches have used the letter: Chrysostom's homilies, Calvin's commentary, the creeds and the kenosis debates over 2:6-11, Catholic and Reformed teaching on what happens at death (1:23), synergy and grace in 2:12-13, the Reformation and Catholic readings of 3:9, Wesley on perfection (3:12), and church order in 1:1.

sections.b:
Read it as a letter between friends. Paul is not defending his authority, as in Galatians or 2 Corinthians; he does not even call himself an apostle. He thanks, reports, encourages and warns, and he expects the Philippians to care about his news as he cares about theirs. Keep the setting in mind: the writer is chained and may be executed, and the readers live in a city that measured people by rank.

Watch for the repeated words. The Plain renders them the same way each time so they can be followed: joy and rejoice; think (the Greek phroneo, a settled way of seeing); partnership and share (koinonia); form (2:6-7; 3:10, 21); low and lowly (2:3, 8; 3:21; 4:12); live as citizens and commonwealth (1:27; 3:20).

The letter opens with a greeting, thanks and prayer (1:1-11), then Paul's news (1:12-26). The main appeal begins at 1:27 and runs through chapter 2: stand together, be humble, think the way that belongs to Christ (the hymn), obey, and look at the examples of Timothy and Epaphroditus. Chapter 3 warns against opponents, most often read as teachers demanding circumcision, through Paul's own story. Chapter 4 makes the appeal personal (Euodia and Syntyche), gives closing commands, thanks the church for its gift, and ends with greetings.

sections.h: Philippians and the rest of the Bible
sections.b: The hymn (2:6-11) takes Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD swears that every knee will bend to him, and applies it to Jesus; Romans 14:11 quotes the same verse of God. Paul's words in 1:19 are the Greek of Job 13:16. 2:14-15 recalls Israel's grumbling in the wilderness and the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5). Paul's credentials (3:5-6) match Romans 11:1, 2 Corinthians 11:22, Galatians 1:13-14 and Acts 22:3 and 23:6. 3:9 belongs with Romans 3:21-22 and Galatians 2:16; 3:21 with 1 Corinthians 15:42-53. Acts 16 tells the founding of the church.

sections.h: Words that are hard to translate
sections.b: Some places in this letter turn on one Greek word, and the Plain has had to choose: morphe 'form' (2:6-7), harpagmos 'something to exploit' (2:6), ekenosen 'emptied' (2:7), pistis Christou 'faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ' (3:9), skybala 'dung' (3:8), politeuma 'commonwealth' (3:20) and syzygos 'yokefellow', perhaps a name (4:3). Each has a note that sets out the other possibilities.

spec.title: Claude's theory: chapter 3 is Paul's own version of the hymn
spec.body: The hymn (2:6-11) and Paul's story (3:4-21) share an unusual set of words: 'count' (2:6; 3:7-8), 'form' (2:6-7; 3:10, 21), 'found' (2:8; 3:9), 'low' (2:8; 3:21), 'outward shape' and 'refashion' (2:8; 3:21), and 'Lord' (2:11; 3:8, 20). In both, a person with high status counts it as nothing to hold onto, goes down to death, and is lifted up by God. If this is deliberate, chapter 3 is not a change of subject but Paul putting himself inside the hymn: he did with his Jewish privileges what Christ did with equality with God. That would be an argument for the letter's unity, since a writer joining fragments would not create such links by chance. Many commentators have noticed some of these links; arranging them as a deliberate retelling across the supposed seam at 3:1 is my own suggestion, and the links could also come from one writer using his favorite words in two letters.

prompts: A small stone room lit by a high window; Paul, an older bearded Jewish man, chained by the wrist to a Roman soldier who dozes on a bench, dictates to a young man (Timothy) writing on papyrus. On a shelf, a small purse and a folded cloak, the gift from Philippi. Sketched by hand onto old rolled parchment with ochre cave-painting figures and soft modern watercolor washes; wobbling ink lines, torn edges; no hard rectangular frame.
The way down and the way up

A V-shaped path drawn across a scroll: at the top left a figure in radiant light, then step by step down the slope into a servant's tunic, to a rough cross at the bottom, then up the right slope to a throne where many small figures bow from heaven, earth and below the earth. Drawn like an ancient manuscript illumination mixed with cave-drawing figures and faded watercolor; parchment texture; soft borders, no sharp frame.

A group of women in Greek and Roman dress sitting on the grassy bank of a small river outside a city gate, one in a purple-dyed shawl listening to a traveler; in the distance the walls of a Roman colony and a Latin inscription on an arch. Sketched in charcoal and ochre on a scroll, with soft modern wash; edges soft and torn.
